newsitem.title: GERMANY: German industry boss wants consensus model reform.
newsitem.headline: German industry boss wants consensus model reform.

text.p: The head of the Federation of German Industry (BDI) said on Tuesday increased globalisation of trade meant the country's renowned collective bargaining between unions and employers was outdated and needed an overhaul.

"We must consider whether the German model of (unions) participating in (company) decision making can survive given increasing European integration and how far it will have to be changed," BDI head Hans-Olaf Henkel told Die Zeit weekly in an interview released ahead of publication on Wednesday.
"It should be clear to us: nobody wants our model any more," Henkel said.
Germany's consensus model of bargaining is credited with years of post-war industrial peace which contributed to the country's so-called economic miracle in the 1950s and 1960s.
But employers argue that unions have become too strong and are now holding back today's unemployment-stricken economy.

Even German unions in recent months have moved away from their strict insistence that centralised wage bargaining must be maintained at all costs and have said they would accept some changes to the model.
They are seeking to link any reform to firm commitments from employer federations on job creation measures against a backdrop of record post-war unemployment.
Henkel said up until now the participation of unions in company decisions had been positive for German industry, but the country now had to have the courage to address the disadvantages of the model.

"What is the result when a globally-orientated company must have participatory decision-making in one country and not in another? It can lead to the rejection (of Germany) in location decisions," Henkel said.
